claims.text: The exceptional ethanol-oxidation performance is governed by a potential-induced transient oxide layer on the platinum-group nanoscale catalyst.
The transient oxide layer tunes the adsorption energies of key ethanol-oxidation intermediates.
Oxide-mediated changes in intermediate adsorption lower activation barriers.
Formation of the transient oxide layer enhances product selectivity and catalyst durability.
The catalyst is a platinum-group-metal-based nanoscale material operated electrochemically.
Systematically changing the applied potential away from an optimal baseline is the controlled intervention.
Applied potential can induce restructuring of the catalyst surface under the proposed ethanol-oxidation conditions.
Changing the potential causes transient formation and modulation of an in situ surface oxide layer.
At the optimal baseline potential, a stable transient oxide layer forms.
The baseline oxide layer produces favorable adsorption energies for intermediates in the 12-electron/12-proton ethanol-oxidation pathway.
Potential deviations disturb the oxide structure and thereby alter intermediate adsorption.
Potential-induced changes in intermediate adsorption alter catalytic performance.
Moving the potential away from the baseline will produce measurable changes in oxide-layer coverage.
Activity, product distribution, and durability will covary with oxide-layer coverage.
Catalytic performance will decline when the oxide layer is either over-developed or under-developed.
A single optimal applied potential provides peak activity, selectivity, and durability while maintaining a stable transient oxide layer.
The proposed mechanism applies only under electrochemical ethanol-oxidation conditions capable of inducing surface restructuring and oxide formation.
The proposed mechanism will not operate under non-electrochemical conditions or in environments that do not promote oxide formation.
Electrocatalysis occurs at the interface between an electrocatalyst surface and an electrolyte.
